title: How the Avocado Went From 'Butter Fruit' to India's Hottest Ingredient
excerpt: Once an obscure tropical fruit sold for ₹40 a kilo in Mangalore, the avocado has become a fixture on Indian restaurant menus and urban grocery shelves — with a push from the Prime Minister himself.
body:
• The avocado, long known as 'butter fruit' in South India, has gone mainstream in Indian urban markets and restaurant menus following years of supply constraints and consumer unfamiliarity.
  • Prime Minister Narendra Modi recently promoted avocado cultivation in a social media post, adding to growing farmer interest in the crop.
  • Indian chefs are innovating beyond standard avocado toast, creating dishes like avocado gilawat kebabs, nimbu masala avocado on papad, and mango makhana avocado chaat.
  • Domestic avocado production is rising as farmers and tea and coffee planters adopt cultivation, though the premium Hass variety introduced in 2017 remains the most in-demand among chefs.

The avocado's journey in India begins with an unlikely connection: a conversation between Paramahansa Yogananda and Mahatma Gandhi in 1935 about whether the creamy fruit could serve as a vegetarian alternative to meat. Gandhi was intrigued enough to accept saplings shipped from Yogananda's California ashram for his Wardha community, but the plants withered in transit. India's avocado moment would have to wait nearly a century.

That moment appears to have arrived. Once an obscure tropical fruit known as 'butter fruit' in the hills of Coorg, Ooty, and Kodaikanal, the avocado has become a staple of urban Indian restaurant menus, café culture, and increasingly, home kitchens.

From ₹40 Per Kilo to Premium Staple

The transformation has been rapid. Chef-restaurateur Bakshish Dean recalls encountering 'butter fruit' in Mangalore in 2014, where it sold for ₹40 per kilo — roughly a fifth of what the Hass variety commands today. The local fruit, however, was unreliable: often unripe, it had to be ripened in rice bags, with many spoiling in the process, and carried a slightly bitter taste that required sugar to mask.

The turning point came with the introduction of Hass avocados into India in 2017. The cultivar, prized globally for its creamy texture and ability to absorb flavors, opened up possibilities that the domestic 'butter fruit' could not. Restaurants that had been limited to imported-avocado guacamole at steep prices suddenly had a viable ingredient for broader menu use.

"No vegetarian menu today is complete without what caterers describe as the BATA items — burrata cheese, avocado, truffles and asparagus."

— Gauri Devidayal, restaurateur and NDTV Food Awards 2026 honoree

Indian Chefs Go Beyond Avo Toast

While avocado toast remains a crowd-pleaser — Gauri Devidayal of Mag St. in Mumbai says she would face a revolt if she removed it from the menu — Indian chefs have been pushing the ingredient into distinctly desi territory.

Chef Chiquita Gulati, formerly of Spice Market in Delhi, created a vegetarian gilawat kebab using avocados with the same masala mix as the famous Lucknowi mutton version. The softness of avocados made the kebabs nearly impossible to flip while sautéing, but she refused to add paneer or potato binders, turning the dish into a signature offering for the vegetarian catering circuit.

At Comorin restaurants, Brand Chef Dhiraj Dargan has created Nimbu Masala Avocado served on Banarasi Aloo Papad, and a Mango Makhana Avocado Chaat with Kokum Dressing. Chef Manish Mehrotra of Nisaba places avocado slices atop chicken dahi bhalla for textural contrast, while at Olive in Delhi, Executive Chef Dhruv Oberoi has developed a fully vegetarian crudo using thinly sliced avocado with ceviche dressing.

The PM's Nudge and Rising Production

Prime Minister Modi recently posted a reel promoting avocado cultivation, a move widely seen as a nudge to Indian farmers to cash in on growing urban demand. Domestic production has been climbing as a growing number of farmers, along with tea and coffee planters in southern hill regions, adopt avocado cultivation.

The supply-side expansion matters. For years, the avocado's presence in Indian cuisine was constrained by irregular supplies and inconsistent quality. Chef Mehrotra recalls first using avocado at a London restaurant in 2006 but being unable to do more with it at Indian Accent in Delhi because reliable supply simply was not there.

With availability improving, the fruit has spread from high-end restaurants to cafés and street vendors. In Surat, street food stalls now serve avocado preparations. In Bandra, Mumbai, café Boojee owes much of its viral popularity to its avo toast variations with hummus, guacamole, and chilli eggs.

As food columnist Sourish Bhattacharyya writes: "You know an ingredient has arrived when it churns the creative juices of chefs." The avocado, once unknown and now drawing attention from the Prime Minister, has arrived in India — on its own Indian terms.

nri_angle: For diaspora Indians familiar with avocado culture in the US and Australia, the fruit's rise in India represents a convergence of global food trends and desi culinary innovation — from gilawat kebabs to avocado chaat.
